transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

I came in because I’ve been feeling pretty hopeless lately. Not in a dramatic way, just this quiet feeling that the best part of my life is behind me, and that no matter how much I plan or try to stay disciplined, I’m not going to get back to feeling like myself.
Did this start after a specific stressful event or major life change?
Yes. It really started after a hiking injury a little over three years ago. So… about three years and three months now.
Are you still feeling this hopeless now?

Yes. It’s still there. It’s not like I’m in a panic about it, but I keep feeling like the better part of my life is behind me, and that no matter how organized or disciplined I try to be, I’m not really going to get back to feeling like myself.
Do you feel this way mainly because of the lasting effects of the hiking injury?
Yes, mostly. It’s been going on since that hiking injury, a little over three years ago now—about three years and three months.
For the past two years, have you felt down or hopeless more days than not?

Yes. Most days it’s there. I’m not crying or falling apart, exactly, but there’s this low, gray feeling underneath things, even when I’m doing something like being in the studio or having dinner with my wife.
Have you lost interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?
I’m not sure I’d say I’ve lost interest exactly. I still do the things I usually enjoy. They just don’t always feel as rewarding as they used to.
Are the ongoing effects of the hiking injury still causing major problems in your daily life?

Yes, it still affects me. I can handle the basic things at home, but my life has gotten smaller. I’ve pulled back from mentoring, community events, music get-togethers, and even travel plans. I’m functioning, but not the way I used to.
Do you still feel this low even on days when the injury is not bothering you much?

Yes. Even when the injury isn’t really acting up, I still feel that low feeling. It’s not like I’m in tears all day, but there’s this gray tone underneath things, even if I’m in the studio or just having dinner with my wife.
During this time, have there been periods when the depression became much worse than your usual low mood?

I don’t know that I’d call it much worse. It’s been more like a steady low mood for a long time. Some days are heavier than others, sure, but I haven’t noticed a clear period where it suddenly got dramatically worse.
Did this low mood begin within three months of your hiking injury?
Yes, it started around then. The injury was a little over three years ago, and this low mood has basically been going on since then — about three years and three months now.
If you imagine that the effects of the hiking injury were completely resolved, do you think this low mood would still be there?

I think it probably would still be there, yes. It doesn’t feel like it’s only about the injury anymore. Most days I’m not crying or anything dramatic, but there’s still this low, gray feeling underneath things, even when I’m doing something normal like working in the studio or having dinner with my wife.
Have you had low energy most days?

Yes, most days I’d say my energy is pretty low. I still get up and do the shopping, and I’ll tinker with projects, but it doesn’t take much to wear me out. Even setting up for a mentoring session or walking around a community event can leave me drained, and a nap doesn’t really fix it.
Do you often feel badly about yourself?
I’m not sure I’d say often. I mean, I have moments where I get down on myself, but it’s not something I notice all the time or could clearly point to as a major issue.
Do you often have trouble concentrating or making decisions?
I’m not really sure. I don’t think I’ve noticed that as a big problem. I can usually follow things and make ordinary decisions, at least as far as I can tell.
During this time, has there ever been a period of at least two weeks when you felt depressed nearly every day?

Yes. I’d say there have been long stretches like that. Most days I’m not crying or anything dramatic, but there’s this low, gray feeling underneath everything, even when I’m in the studio or having dinner with my wife.
Over the past two years, have there been any stretches longer than two months when you did not feel depressed or hopeless?

No, I don’t think there’s been a stretch that long. It’s been going on since I hurt myself hiking a little over three years ago—about three years and three months now. Some days are better than others, but I can’t point to two months where it really lifted.
During those two-week periods when your depression felt present nearly every day, did your appetite change noticeably?
I’m not sure. I don’t think my appetite changed in any clear way during those times. Nothing that really stood out to me.
During those times when you felt depressed nearly every day, did your sleep change noticeably?
I don’t really know. I haven’t noticed a clear change in my sleep during those periods. It’s not something that stands out to me.
During the times when you felt depressed nearly every day, did you eat less than usual?
I don’t think so. I haven’t noticed that I was eating less than usual during those times.
During those times when you felt depressed nearly every day, did your weight change noticeably?
No, not that I can tell. My weight’s been pretty much the same, or at least I haven’t noticed any noticeable change during those periods.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a chronic depressed/hopeless mood present most days for over 3 years, beginning within months of a hiking injury but persisting independently of the injury, with no remission longer than 2 months. Associated symptoms include low energy and reduced sense of reward/pleasure, with clear functional contraction in social/community/professional activities. There is no evidence of distinct major depressive episodes with marked worsening or sufficient neurovegetative symptom burden, making persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) the best fit over single/recurrent major depressive disorder or unspecified anxiety disorder.
